Distance-aware index sorting optimizes sorting by computing distance data once and using an auxiliary structure to avoid redundant calculations during comparison [S2, unofficial].

The claim states that distance-aware index sorting optimizes sorting by computing distance data once and using an auxiliary structure to avoid redundant calculations. Source [S2] explicitly suggests this exact optimization: computing the distance squared from the origin once for all blocks, storing it in an auxiliary structure (`DistanceIndexPair`), sorting that structure, and then mapping the results back. This matches the claim's description of computing data once and using an auxiliary structure to avoid redundant calculations (specifically, avoiding calling `relativeToOrigin` twice per comparison).

The method was analyzed on NVIDIA GTX 280 hardware, demonstrating that while naive index sorting suffers from performance penalties, optimized coalesced approaches mitigate these issues [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly mentions the 'GTX 280' hardware in the context of performance analysis. It states that typical radix index sorting suffers a performance reduction by a factor of 1.5 to 1.8 (performance penalties) due to non-coalesced shuffling. It further states that applying the coalesced radix index sorting scheme reduces this penalty to a negligible factor of about 1.1 (mitigates these issues). All factual components of the claim are present in the provided text.
supported
Index sorting avoids this by keeping them separate, allowing full 32-bit index ranges [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that index sorting avoids precision loss (implied by 'this' in context of combining value and index) by keeping them separate, allowing full 32-bit index ranges. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly states: 'Unlike methods that combine value and index into the same sorting register (which reduces precision and index range), this approach keeps key counting independent, allowing up to 4 billion key-index pairs on 32-bit GPUs.' Since 4 billion corresponds to the full 32-bit range (2^32), the evidence fully supports the claim.
